turns.doctor_question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello. Thank you for seeing me. I suppose... well, I came in because things have just been so incredibly tense at work lately, and I just don't know how to process it all anymore. I’m a secondary school teacher—history, mostly the older years, which is a handful on its own, as you can imagine. I've been teaching for over thirty years now, so I know how schools operate. I know the rhythms of the day, the administrative side of things, all of it. 

But recently, maybe over the last few months or so, there’s been this... well, a shift. It started with the morning announcements over the PA system. You know, the usual things the headmaster reads out about assembly times or parking lot rules or cafeteria menus. But I started noticing—and I still can't shake this feeling, no matter how much I try to just sit at my desk and focus on my lesson plans—that they aren't just general announcements. The phrasing they use, the specific pauses, the choice of words... it feels quite clearly like they are actually coded messages directed specifically at me. Like a warning, or some sort of commentary on what I'm doing, hidden right there out in the open where the students can't catch on but I'm supposed to. 

And it’s not just the intercom, either. It’s the staff emails. I’ll read a memo about, say, the new grading software or a reminder about locking the supply cupboards, and I can just tell that between the lines, it’s a message meant only for me. I actually brought it up in the staff room the other day to Margaret—she teaches geography next door to me, lovely woman, we’ve shared a wall for a decade—and she was very gentle about it. She actually pulled up her laptop right there by the kettle and showed me the header of the email, pointing out that it was sent to the entire "All Staff" mailing list. She kept saying, "Look, we all got the exact same email, it's just standard administrative nonsense." 

And logically, I look at her screen, I see the email addresses... but the feeling just doesn't go away. Even when they show me it went to everyone, I can't stop feeling like the message itself was written *for* me, and just disguised as a mass email to throw me off. It's just exhausting, frankly, trying to decipher what they really want from me from the moment the first bell rings to the end of the day.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed belief that general school announcements and mass staff emails contain coded messages directed specifically at them, which persists even when a colleague provides contradictory evidence.

turns.doctor_question: Have you been diagnosed with any medical or neurological illness?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, nothing of the sort. I mean, I suppose it’s almost a miracle, given the environment I work in. You’d think being surrounded by hundreds of teenagers for three decades would leave you with every ailment in the book, but I’ve always been very diligent about my health. 

I see my regular GP—Dr. Evans, he’s been my doctor for ages—every August right before the autumn term begins. I always do it then because once September starts, well, you know how it is, there’s simply no time to be sitting around in waiting rooms when you have a syllabus to launch. And he’s always told me my health is perfectly fine. My blood pressure is excellent, surprisingly, especially for a teacher, and I’ve certainly never had to see a neurologist or get any sort of brain scan or anything like that. 

There's no history of seizures or strokes or... well, whatever else falls under that umbrella. I don't even get headaches, really, unless I've been staring at Year 11 essays for too many hours without my reading glasses. So physically, medically speaking, my record is completely clean. I haven't even taken a sick day for a physical illness since a rather nasty bout of bronchitis back in, oh, it must have been 2017. So no, absolutely nothing diagnosed. My brain and my body are perfectly healthy. It’s really just this... this intense, exhausting situation with the messages at the school that’s wearing me down, not my physical health.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing these messages as being directed specifically at you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... let me think. We are in late summer now, so... it would have been right around the middle of the spring term. Yes, just before the Easter holidays, actually. I remember it quite vividly because I was in the thick of marking the Year 11 mock exams—which is always an incredibly demanding period, as you can imagine, just mountains of paper everywhere on my desk—and that’s when the worries about the coded messages really began to take hold. 

So, let's see... April, May, June, July... it’s been about four months. Four months of this constant, daily analyzing of every single word that comes out of that PA system or lands in my inbox. And, actually, now that I’m really thinking about that specific timeframe and how it all started, it wasn't just the messages that began then. It was also right around that exact same time, maybe just a week or so after the intercom announcements started feeling so pointed, that I started... well, I started noticing this voice. 

It's just a voice, and I find myself sometimes answering it, just talking back to it when I'm alone in my classroom after the students have gone home for the day and the corridors are finally quiet. It’s a bit strange to admit out loud, I suppose, but yes, both the worries about the coded messages and that voice I sometimes answer, they’ve both been happening for about four months now. 

And I must say, these last four months have felt much more like four years, what with the constant vigilance it all requires. You just never really get a moment's peace when you're constantly trying to figure out what they are trying to tell you through the morning announcements, or when you're suddenly responding to someone who isn't standing there in the room with you. It really takes a toll on your energy, especially when you still have to stand up and deliver a comprehensive lecture on the Tudor dynasty the very next morning...

turns.doctor_question: Have the voice and the sense that these messages are meant specifically for you been happening continuously for more than one month?
turns.patient_response:
Yes, oh absolutely, yes. It hasn't stopped at all. Like I said, it started right around the Easter holidays, which feels like a lifetime ago now, but it's been about four months. Four entire months of this. And it hasn't been something that comes and goes, you know? It's not like I have a good week where I don't hear the voice or where the morning announcements just sound like normal announcements. It is every single day. 

I wake up, I have my tea, I drive to work, and from the absolute second I step out of my car in the staff car park, I am on edge, waiting for the PA system to crackle to life, waiting for that voice to chime in while I'm trying to organize my desk. It’s a continuous, unbroken chain of days. I mean, even on the weekends, when I'm not at the school, I'll be at home trying to grade papers or do a bit of gardening, and the voice is still there, and I'll find myself answering it while I'm pruning the hydrangeas. And I'll still be agonizing over an email that was sent on Friday afternoon, trying to decode it. So yes, it has definitely been well over a month. Four months, continuously, without a single day's reprieve. It’s just relentless, really.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed yourself becoming much less motivated or emotionally expressive than usual?
turns.patient_response:
Well, now that you mention it... yes, I suppose I have. Though it's difficult to pinpoint exactly when it started, but it's been going on for many months now. I still care, you know? I really do. I care deeply about my students—I always have, that's why I've stayed in the profession so long—and I care about my friends. But it’s as if... well, it’s like the warmth and the drive have just completely drained out of me. 

I used to be so involved in things outside of the classroom. I was the one who always organized our monthly book club meetings—I’d pick the book, arrange the venue, sometimes even bake something for us all to share. And I was always heavily involved in the theater planning committee at school, helping with the costumes and the set design for the spring musical. I took such pride in it. But lately... I just let it all slide. I haven't attended book club since... oh, it must be before Christmas. I just couldn't muster the energy to read the book, let alone go and discuss it. And the theater committee... I just quietly stopped going to the meetings. 

Even simple things, like making a phone call to my sister on a Sunday afternoon, which used to be a weekly ritual for us. Now, I just... I look at the phone and I can't bring myself to dial the number. I just sit there. Unless someone really pushes me, unless someone physically comes up to me and says, "We need you to do this right now," I just don't have the motivation to initiate anything anymore. It’s not that I don't want to see my friends or talk to my family, it’s just this... this profound emptiness, like my battery is completely flat and refuses to recharge. I just feel so incredibly flat, emotionally speaking, like all the color has washed out of everything. It’s quite sad, really, when I say it out loud like that, but yes, it’s been months of just feeling completely depleted of any sort of spark or enthusiasm.
